description: Team30 builds novel systems - we combine hardware, AI, and UI/UX to transform technical challenges into functional solutions.
summary:
The Crew State Observation System (CSOS) is a wearable device designed to monitor the health of crew's members working in extreme environments, especially astronauts during space missions. Worn on the forearm, it collects important body measurements, such as skin temperature, pressure, muscle activity (EMG), heart rate, blood oxygen levels (SpO₂), blood flow, and humidity beneath the device.

The collected data is analyzed by the system: the software reduces noise caused by movement, tracks changes in the member's condition, and detects possible anomalies. If something unusual is found, the system provides access to relevant first-aid instructions from its built-in medical reference database.

One of the main advantages of CSOS is that it works completely offline, without depending on the connection to Earth or cloud services. This makes it useful for long-term space missions and other remote environments where communication and immediate medical assistance may not always be available. The goal is to help crew members notice potential health problems earlier and have useful medical information available when they need it most.
details:
What does the project do and how does it work?

The Crew State Observation System (CSOS) is a wearable device for monitoring the condition of people working in extreme environments, particularly astronauts during space missions.

The device is worn on the forearm and combines several types of sensors to collect important telemetry. These include skin temperature, local pressure, muscle activity (EMG), heart rate, blood oxygen saturation (SpO₂), blood-flow dynamics, and humidity beneath the device.

The system uses a microcontroller to accumulate sensor data and transmit it via WLAN to a host computer. The software processes the measurements and identifies changes in the user’s physical condition.

If an abnormality is detected, the system picks out relevant first-aid instructions from its built-in medical reference database.

An important feature of CSOS is that all functions work locally, without depending on a connection or cloud services.

What benefits does the project have?

One of the main features is that CSOS allows several parameters to be monitored using a single device. This reduces the need for multiple separate instruments.

Continuous monitoring can help identify changes in a person’s physical condition earlier and mitigate possible health problems before they become more serious.

Another advantage is the offline medical reference system. Instead of simply displaying measurements, CSOS can provide first-aid information about a particular problem.

This is particularly valuable in space missions and remote environments, where access to immediate medical assistance may be limited.

What is the intended impact of the project?

The main goal of CSOS is to improve crew safety by providing a complete picture of a person’s physical condition.

The system is primarily created for astronaut health monitoring, but its applications are not limited to spaceflight. It could also be useful in isolated research facilities, extreme-environment operations, and other situations where offline health monitoring is crucial.

In the long term, we hope that this project can contribute to the development of autonomous health monitoring systems that help people recognize potential problems and access medical information when professional assistance is not immediately available.

What tools, programming languages, hardware, and software were used?

Programming languages and software tools:

  • Visual Studio Code as main worktable
  • Python for physiological data processing and analysis
  • C/C++ via PlatformIO for embedded firmware development
  • Large Language Models for debugging and automating routine code

In the current version, only app demo is finished. We used the list of libraries:

PyMuPDF [PDF viewer tool]

customtkinter [The main graphics library]

pillow [UI images manipulating]

pyqtgraph [Real-time plotting & visualisation]

matplotlib [Static and dynamic plotting]

pyserial [Data receiving]

numpy, pandas [Arrays and complex math structures]

scipy [Common signal processing and analysis]

neurokit2 [Optical data conversion]

biosppy [EMG processing]

The device (hardware) in the prototype is only ESP32 that imitates sensors and sends synthetic data. However, the concept of the device has a list of particular professional sensors:

TMP117 x4 - Temperature sensors

BMP390 x4 - Barometers

ADS1298 x6 - Electromyographs (EMG)

MAX86141 x2 - Optical biometry (HR, SpO2, Blood flow)

, components:

Saft MP 144350 - Solid-state accumulator (3.75V 2.6Ah)

BQ27441-G1 - Fuel gauging for a battery (Charge level)

, and ideas:

Wireless charging - Isolated wireless coils for convenient charging the module

Protected hardware radiomodule - For reliable data transmission

Professional production FPGA - Instead of ESP32 as the main data gatherer.

According to datasheets, the estimated work time of the device is approximately 7 days on a single charge.

The communication is based on local wireless transmission and uses principles of Space Packet Protocol from CCSDS wireless packet standards (exact Primary Header format and configuration).

How is the project creative and innovative?

What makes CSOS different is the fact that it merges hardware monitoring devices, a processing app and offline medical resources into one system.

Many health monitoring devices focus mainly on basic measurements such as heart rate or blood oxygen levels. CSOS reads a broader range of parameters - from external conditions to blood characteristics.

Another feature is the built-in first-aid reference system. The device not only collects telemetry but also identifies unusual changes and retrieves relevant information from a database.

We also focused on making the system independent of external infrastructure. Its monitoring and guidance functions are designed to be available even in the absence of a connection to Earth.

The combination of multi-sensor monitoring, autonomous analysis, and integrated medical reference assistance is what makes CSOS a novel approach to crew health monitoring.

What factors did the team consider during development?

We carefully looked for any vulnerabilities that can appear in the current concept. We encountered some factors and paid attention to them:

  • Offline operation: Designed the system to remain functional and reliable without relying on connectivity or cloud servers.
  • Local network reliability: Explored how local wireless communication on and around the space station works.
  • Power consumption: Optimized power usage so the device can operate continuously on a single charge without recharging.
  • Data coverage: Gathered a wide range of physical parameters for an exhaustive analysis.
  • Sensor selection: Chose professional reliable components and sensors.
  • Ergonomics & comfort: Designed the device to be wearable on the forearm so it does not interfere with an astronaut's daily tasks or mobility.

Conclusion

The Crew State Observation System is a platform, where light wearable devices turn into understandable health data for instant actions.

Our aim is to develop a system that helps monitor crew members’ conditions, identify concerning changes, and make medical information available while immediate assistance is not.

Ultimately, CSOS is designed around one important idea: in extreme environments, reliable information about a person’s physical condition should always be accessible, even in space, at the Arctic pole, or in the depths of the sea.
